1.pericope_label: Moses at a hundred and twenty takes his leave and names the Lord as Israel's leader

schools.summary: Gill reconstructs the movement behind the opening verb: after making the covenant he was directed to make, Moses dismissed the people to their tents and went to his own, and now returns, having ordered them to meet him again, probably at the tabernacle, with which the Targum of Jonathan agrees in saying he went to the tabernacle of the house of doctrine, while Aben Ezra reads it of his going to each tribe as they lay encamped, to tell them he was about to die and strengthen their hearts. Calvin asks why addresses so far from gratifying, full of threats and reproofs, had to be heard from Moses' own mouth, and answers that had they been delivered after his death the people would have exclaimed that they were devised by someone else and his name falsely attached to them; the moment added weight of another kind, for we know with what attention the last words of the dying are received. He also draws the general lesson from the naming of a successor: whenever God raises up men endowed with excellent gifts He so uses their labours for a time as still to retain others in His hand, so that His power is not tied to the illustrious qualities of men, as though their death were His destruction.

Henry hears reluctance in the repeated farewells: Moses was loth to part, not because he was loth to go to God but because he was loth to leave them, fearing that when he had left them they would leave God. Though Joshua was continued to fight for them in the valley, they would want Moses to intercede on the hill as at Rephidim; and the sentence that he should not go over Jordan put a full stop to his usefulness — hitherto he must serve, but no further. Henry knows no reason why any of us should desire to live longer than while God has work for us to do.

Clarke observes that the lawgiver's life was exactly the length of time Noah employed in preaching righteousness to the antediluvian world, and divides it into three periods of forty: forty years in Egypt in Pharaoh's court, acquiring the learning and wisdom of the Egyptians; forty in Midian in preparation for his mission; and forty guiding Israel under the express authority of God. Wesley glosses the inability to go out and come in more narrowly, as the loss of ability to perform the office of a leader or governor.

Keil guards the first of Moses' two reasons against the later statement that his eye was not dim nor his natural force abated: that is merely an affirmation that he retained the ability to see and to work to the last moment of his life, which by no means precludes his noticing the decline of his strength and feeling death approach. On the promise itself he is plain: the Lord would go before Israel and destroy the Canaanites as He had the two kings of the Amorites, Israel's part being to do to them as commanded.

debates.question: Why does Moses say he can no more go out and come in, when his sight and strength were unabated to the end?

positions.position: the words affirm only that he could see and work to the last moment, and do not preclude his feeling the decline of his strength
not that his eyes were dim or his members tremulous, but that his age no longer allowed the usual duties; having reached the end of his course he must suddenly sink

themes: I am an hundred and twenty years old this day
I can no more go out and come in
the Lord thy God, he will go over before thee

4.pericope_label: Be strong and of a good courage: the charge to Israel and to Joshua

schools.summary: Calvin reads the appeal to Sihon and Og as an argument from experience: as God had delivered the two Amorite kings into their hands, so He would give the same success against the rest, for though the world is subject to many revolutions God remains like Himself, His counsel never changed and His power never diminished. In appearance, he grants, the command was fierce and cruel, to leave not one alive; but since God had justly devoted them to extinction it was not lawful for Israel to inquire what was to be done, but to abandon all discussion and obey. On the promise attached to the charge he presses further: the people were animated to perseverance of hope by God's declaring that He would be their helper even to the end, and by that the hallucination is refuted whereby theologians deny that believers can be certain of God's grace except as to their present state. Gill notes that where the Lord is said to give them up before Israel's face, the Targum of Jonathan reads the Word of the Lord shall deliver them up, and turns the Septuagint's play the man into being strong in the Lord and in the power of his might.

Clarke observes that the verb rendered be strong is the one used in Exodus for the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, and that the Septuagint renders both this verse and the next play the man and be strong — whence St. Paul seems to have borrowed his words to the Corinthians: stand firm in the faith, play the man, be vigorous. He takes the four clauses of the last verse one by one: He will go before thee, to prepare thy way; be with thee in all thy journeys and enterprises; not fail thee, for thy expectation cannot be too large; not forsake thee, since without Him thou canst do nothing, and He will continue with thee in such a manner that the excellence of the power shall appear to be of Him and not of man.

Keil defends the received reading of the promise to Joshua, thou wilt come with this people into the land: the emendation that would make it thou wilt bring, after a later verse, is an unnecessary conjecture, since Joshua is not appointed leader here but simply promised an entrance with all the people.

outliers.observation: That Moses turns from the nation to one man shows that a public charge needs a twofold confirmation, since it is harder to lead all the rest than to follow a leader; and the fear forbidden is not feeling but its mastery — Calvin will not have them so deprived of sense as to be hardened into indifference to danger, or suppose with certain madmen that there is no bravery without stupidity.

themes: he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee
fear not, nor be afraid of them
thou shalt cause them to inherit it

9.pericope_label: Moses writes the law and commits it to the priests and the elders

schools.summary: Gill takes this law for the book of Deuteronomy, or else the whole Pentateuch, the five books which taken together are sometimes so called. Calvin infers a standing duty from the mere fact of the deposit: though it is only related that the Levites were commanded to recite the book every seventh year, it would have been absurd that the Law should lie buried seven whole years together and not a word of its instruction be heard, so that they were appointed rather as guardians of the Law, of whom the people might daily inquire the right way of serving God. In this he sees represented as in a mirror what Paul calls the Church, the pillar and ground of the truth, since purity of doctrine is preserved and propagated by the ministry of pastors and piety would soon decay if the living preaching of doctrine should cease. The naming of the elders beside the priests is not superfluous: Calvin makes them coadjutors rather than teachers, given to uphold the doctrine of the Law and not suffer it to be scorned, since we know how great is the insolence of the people in rejecting pious teachers unless those in authority restrain them.

Henry reports that Bishop Patrick understood all five books, supposing that though Moses had written most of them before, he did not finish till now and here put his last hand to that sacred volume, while many take it of Deuteronomy alone, this grand abridgment of the law. He gives two reasons for the writing: that those who had heard it might often review it themselves, and that it might be the more safely handed down to posterity — the church has received abundance of advantage from the writing as well as the preaching of divine things, for faith comes not only by hearing but by reading, and the same care taken of the law was taken of the gospel, which soon after it was preached was written. From the elders' inclusion he infers that magistrates by their power, as well as ministers by their doctrine, are to maintain religion and take care that the law be neither broken nor lost.

Clarke rejects one rabbinic tradition and accepts another. That Moses wrote thirteen copies, one for each of the twelve tribes and a thirteenth to be laid up by the ark, deserves little credit; that he wrote two is likely, since the law was properly a covenant or contract between God and the people, and it is natural to suppose each contracting party had one — the copy laid beside the ark being the Lord's, kept as a standard for reference and a witness against the people should they become idolatrous, and the copy given to the priests and Levites being the people's, for general use. Wesley reads the charge to the priests as the practical half of the same thing: they were to keep it carefully and religiously, bring it forth upon occasion, read it, and instruct the people out of it.

debates.question: What is the law that Moses wrote?

positions.position: the whole Pentateuch, finished and put into final shape at this point
the discourses of this book alone, which is a grand abridgment of the law

themes: Moses wrote this law, and delivered it unto the priests
the sons of Levi, which bare the ark of the covenant
and unto all the elders of Israel

10.pericope_label: The septennial reading at the feast of tabernacles, to men, women, children and strangers

schools.summary: Calvin traces the writing itself to the fear of forgetting: before this the doctrines of religion had only been expressed by word of mouth, so that faith in Egypt rested only on ancient revelations and their fathers' traditions, but since nothing is easier than for men's minds to forget true doctrine and involve themselves in manifold errors, God consigned the rule of piety to public records, that there might be no pretence of ignorance if their posterity declined from it. The deposit with one tribe he explains by the same knowledge of men: had Moses exhorted all indifferently to read it, scarcely any would have applied themselves. That such precautions still failed appals him — nothing is too sacred or too well fortified to escape man's wickedness, since with the recitation thus precisely enjoined it was astonishing that the Law should be, as it were, discovered in the time of Josiah. He will not let the mention of women and children pass as a formality: they are named lest age or sex be pleaded as an excuse, and the strangers are not those come into Canaan on business but those who had settled and by long residence coalesced into one body with Israel. Gill notes the difference from the other festivals, that at the three grand feasts only the males were obliged to appear, whereas here all of every age and sex were assembled.

Clarke explains the choice of the sabbatical year by the temper it produced: in the year of release the people's minds, under a peculiar degree of solemnity, were better disposed to hear and profit by the words of God — and on that ground he takes the whole book of Deuteronomy to be meant, since it alone contains an epitome of the Pentateuch. He then observes that the commandment was rarely attended to: from the first public reading under Joshua to the reign of Jehoshaphat he finds none recorded, a period of five hundred and thirty years; the next was not till the eighteenth year of Josiah, two hundred and eighty-two years later; none other is mentioned till the return from the Babylonish captivity under Nehemiah, and none from then to the destruction of Jerusalem. Wesley adds that in that year they were freed from debts and worldly cares, and thereby fitter to attend on God's service, and takes both reading and gathering distributively: thou shalt read means thou shalt cause it to be read by the priests or Levites, and the people were gathered not into one place but into divers assemblies.
Keil fixes the occasion: the reading was to fall at the end of every seven years, in the festal season of the year of release, at the feast of tabernacles, when they appeared before the Lord.

outliers.observation: The stated fruit is that by hearing they might learn to fear God, whence Calvin infers that true religion has its origin in knowledge, and that whatever piety men not instructed by God's word appear to have is mere pretence.

themes: at the end of every seven years, in the solemnity of the year of release
gather the people together, men, and women, and children
that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the Lord your God

14.pericope_label: The Lord appears in the pillar of cloud and calls Moses and Joshua to the tabernacle

schools.summary: Calvin reads the appearance at the door as an act of consecration: Joshua is substituted in the place of Moses by a solemn ceremony, not only that he may be held in greater reverence by men, but that he may be presented before God and so acknowledge himself dedicated to His service. The cloud served both the man and the nation, since the appearance of the glory of God was not less effectual for encouraging Joshua personally than for giving public distinction to his office — he would never have been recognised as Moses' successor unless this visible approbation had fastened the yoke upon the people. Gill notes only what the sign contained: the Lord appeared as he was wont to do, and in the cloud there was a lustre, a brightness, a glory visible, which showed that he was there.

Henry hears in the summons a second warning to a man already prepared: Moses is told again that he must shortly die, for even those most ready to die have need to be often reminded of death's approach, and in consideration of it he must come himself to meet God, since whatever improves our communion with God furthers our preparation for death. He obeys readily, being not one of those who look with an evil eye upon their successors but rejoicing in him. From the rarity of the theophany Henry draws a conclusion: this is the only time in all this book that we read of the glory of God appearing, whereas we often read of it in the three foregoing books, which perhaps signifies that in the latter days, under the evangelical law, such visible appearances are not to be expected, but that we must take heed to the more sure word of prophecy. On the coming breach he notes where the blame must lie — if the covenant between God and man be broken, it is man that breaks it, for God never leaves any till they first leave him.
Wesley takes the charge as issuing directly from God for Joshua's greater encouragement, and to gain him more authority with the people.

Ellicott states what the meeting accomplishes, that what Moses had already done before Israel is now ratified by Jehovah to Joshua and to Moses himself, and sets the scene beside two others of the same kind: Aaron and Eleazar going up Mount Hor together, that the priesthood might be transferred from the one to the other, and Elijah and Elisha crossing Jordan together when Elijah was about to depart. He also marks what closes here — for the last time it is recorded that Jehovah met Moses face to face in the tabernacle, the next meeting being on Mount Nebo, and the next within the veil.

outliers.observation: Their apostasy is foretold as the effect of their prosperity, since they shall have eaten and filled themselves and waxed fat, security taking off their dread of God's judgments and sensuality inclining them to the idolatries of the heathen; and justly does He cast off those who had so unjustly cast Him off, His providence forsaking them so that they become a prey to their neighbours, and His grace forsaking them so that they grow more hardened.

themes: thy days approach that thou must die
present yourselves in the tabernacle of the congregation
the pillar of the cloud stood over the door of the tabernacle

16.pericope_label: Thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, and this people will go a whoring after strange gods

schools.summary: Calvin takes the same words for consolation on both counts: first the condition of the human race is stated, that Moses may not think it hard to depart from the world like all others, but the difference between the death of men and of the brute animals is indicated at the same time, for if our death were total annihilation we should not be said to sleep with our fathers. He also hears an antithesis between the lying down and the rising up — as soon as Moses has gone to rest, the people's insubordination shall break forth, as though they were released from all laws — and counts the aggravations of the crime foretold: they would be led away not only into the superstitions learnt in Egypt but into the defilements of Canaan, which God had willed should be purged by their own hand. Whoever turn aside to superstitious worship are covenant breakers, and vain are the pretences of all who profess to worship the supreme God together with idols. Gill measures the kindled anger by the nearest human likeness, the anger of a man against a wife who has treacherously departed from him.

Clarke notes that the Hebrew verb means to lie down, to rest, to take rest in sleep, and metaphorically to die; and he warns that much stress cannot safely be laid on it to prove the immortality of the soul, or that the people in Moses' time had a distinct notion of its separate existence. It was, however, so understood by Jonathan ben Uzziel, whose Targum paraphrases it: thou shalt lie down in the dust with thy fathers, and thy soul shall be laid up in the treasury of the life to come with thy fathers. Wesley finds a further folly in the object of the worship, since the strangers of the land are the Canaanites, turned out of their possessions and become strangers in their own land, so that Israel would serve gods which could neither preserve their friends nor annoy their enemies; and with Clarke he reads the hidden face as the withdrawal of favour, help, approbation and protection.

Against the broken covenant Ellicott sets a promise in identical Hebrew, the angel's word at Bochim, I said, I will never break my covenant with you, and beside it the apostle's rule that if we believe not, yet He abideth faithful, for He cannot deny Himself. On the hidden face he cites Rashi: as though I did not see them in their distress.

outliers.observation: Calvin finds a use even in punishment that fails to reform: the first step of prudence is voluntarily to choose what is right, the second to make a stand against evil once admonition has been heard, but if reproofs profit nothing there is still a third, that those careless in prosperity should at length perceive they are smitten by God's hand — scarcely one in ten of the godly anticipates judgment while God postpones punishment.

themes: this people will rise up, and go a whoring after the gods of the strangers
my anger shall be kindled against them in that day
are not these evils come upon us, because our God is not among us?

19.pericope_label: Write ye this song and teach it the children of Israel, that it may be a witness

schools.summary: Calvin faces the harder question the command raises. It seems absurd that a useless remedy should be applied to an incurable disease: why not rather correct their wickedness and by His Spirit mould their hearts, than pour words in vain into deaf ears? But the preaching of the word, though a savour of death to them that perish, is a sacrifice of sweet savour to God, and is not thrown away when it convicts the ungodly and renders them altogether inexcusable. On the promise of the good land he marks the aggravation, that God will perform to them, unworthy as they are, what He has sworn, and commends the land's fertility because that pledge of His indulgence should have drawn them to love so beneficent a Father — whence their perverseness appears, that when full they would kick against Him, like horses grown intractable from high feeding. Gill records what Josephus reports of the writing: that Moses set it down in hexameter verse and left it in the sacred book, a prophecy of things future according to which all things have been done and are done, in nothing erring from the truth.

Henry notes the order of publication: he wrote it first, as the Spirit of God indited it, then spoke it in the ears of all the congregation and taught it, that is, gave out copies and ordered the people to learn it by heart.

Clarke explains why the warning takes the form of a song: things of great importance were among the ancients put into verse, as the best method of keeping them in remembrance when writing was little practised, and even prose was sometimes sung — the history of Herodotus being divided into nine books each inscribed with a Muse's name because they were anciently sung, Homer reported to have sung his poems through the Greek cities, Aristotle observing that the people anciently sung their laws, and Cicero that the Romans sang their heroes' praises at the public festivals. He also explains how a song can testify: their general defection is predicted in it, but so as to show how the evil might be avoided, so that if the punishment did come the song would prove they had been sufficiently warned and might have lived to God and escaped. Wesley glosses the imagination as inclinations to idolatry which they do not check, some not only cherishing it in their hearts but, so far as they dared, secretly practising it.

Ellicott adds that the method suited the people better than a written law, since copies could not be multiplied to any great extent, whereas the rhythmical form was easy to retain in memory; and he believes Samuel, the first known to have effected anything toward a system of religious education in Israel, used the same means, the earliest companies of prophets being evidently singers and minstrels — whence their influence over Saul — so that in teaching the people historical psalms such as the seventy-eighth and the hundred and sixth, a very efficacious means of spreading the knowledge of God lay in their hands. He takes up the word rendered imagination, used of the thoughts of man's heart before the flood: it is the term commonly used in rabbinical literature for the evil or the good nature in a man, and the nature which they are forming this day would be a literal rendering here.

themes: put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness
they shall have eaten and filled themselves, and waxen fat
I know their imagination which they go about, even now

23.pericope_label: The charge to Joshua, the book laid beside the ark, and I know thy rebellion

schools.summary: Gill works through a real question, who speaks the charge to Joshua: the connection favours Moses, the nearer antecedent of the pronoun, and the Septuagint translators so understood it, but they were then obliged to alter what follows, reading the Lord sware for I sware; Aben Ezra reaches the same sense without departing from the genuine reading by supposing Moses gave the charge in the name and by the authority of the Lord, though Gill judges it best to understand the Lord himself as the speaker, since it was He who ordered the two to present themselves before Him for this very purpose. By the words of this law Calvin understands not only this book but the other three, and finds an implied antithesis between the two tables written by God's hand and the exposition afterwards added, lest there should be obscurity about God's will from the brevity with which it was delivered — since the mind of man is inclined to vanity and led away by its levity, religion would have been corrupted a thousand ways had not its rule been written down for posterity. He also explains why the law is cited here only as a witness, when it was given rather as the rule of a pious life: Moses had found the people stiffnecked, and argues from the less to the greater, since if they were rebellious while such a leader lived they would assume greater audacity when he was dead.

Henry ends where Moses does, with the plain word that after his death they would utterly corrupt themselves: many a sad thought it cost him, but his comfort was that he had done his duty and that God would be glorified in their dispersion if not in their settlement, for the foundation of God stands sure.

Wesley explains the deposit: the book lay outside, in a little chest fixed to the ark, since nothing but the tables of stone were contained within, and kept there for greater security and reverence; and he guesses it was the very copy which, after being some way misplaced, was found in the house of the Lord in the days of Josiah and read publicly by the king himself, against a people then almost ripe for ruin. Clarke turns the rebellion foretold toward the reader: never was a people more fully warned, and from that we may see they were under no fatal constraining necessity to sin, since they might have avoided it but would not — and those who abuse God's grace shall not only have it taken from them but be punished for the abuse as well as the transgression, since every sin is double, grace resisted and transgression committed, and God will visit for both.

Ellicott says what is new in the moment: this is the first record of God's direct communion with Joshua, who had been with Moses on the mount during the first forty days and departed not out of the tabernacle when they came down, yet of whom no divine communication apart from Moses is noted before this. Keil reads the next summons as following directly on the handing over: the call to gather was addressed to the very persons to whom Moses had given the book, the elders of all the tribes with the officers, who as the civil authorities of the congregation were collected round him to hear the ode rehearsed.

outliers.observation: Gill leaves the question of the speaker argued rather than settled: he judges it best to understand the Lord himself, but records that the Septuagint translators took it of Moses and were then obliged to alter what follows, and that Aben Ezra kept the genuine reading by supposing Moses spoke in the name and by the authority of the Lord.

themes: be strong and of a good courage: for thou shalt bring the children of Israel
put it in the side of the ark of the covenant
I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck

28.pericope_label: The elders gathered, heaven and earth called to record, and the song spoken in their ears

schools.summary: Moses seems to contradict himself, Calvin observes, when he commands only the elders and the officers to be called to listen, and then records that he recited the song to the whole congregation; the two are reconciled from the order he was accustomed to observe in gathering the multitude, for they were not called together promiscuously, but the heads of tribes and the princes each led their own band, so that the assembling of the elders rather indicates that the whole people were gathered by their tribes and classes — and he assuredly did not call heaven and earth to record against the officers only. On the tone of the address Calvin is candid about what it cost: it was the perverse nature of the people which extorted from Moses that unmixed bitterness, since he would have desired to leave a pleasing recollection of himself and to exhort them with blandness, but their stubbornness compelled him to testify his indignation. Nor does he judge from conjecture what they would do, but expressly declares that he knew it for certain, because the Spirit in dictating the song had also informed him of it. Gill reaches the same place from the other side: the words were spoken not in the hearing of every individual of that vast body, since no man could be heard by so numerous a congregation, but in the hearing of their heads and representatives.

Ellicott examines the phrase in the latter days, a not uncommon prophetical expression used with considerable latitude, which occurs for the first time in Jacob's blessing and again in Balaam's oracle and earlier in this book; some would refer it to the days of the Messiah and make it almost a technical term, but a comparison of these few passages shows that it cannot be tied strictly to any one period. He closes the chapter with a symmetry — the exodus of Israel begins and ends with a song of Moses, for though the song at the Red Sea is the one usually so called and commonly thought to be the song named in the Revelation, there is a remarkable resemblance between that passage and the opening lines of the song about to follow here. Keil marks the last verse as the introduction to the rehearsal of the ode.

outliers.observation: Calvin reads the manner of the corruption out of the words themselves: they would depart from the way which they had learned, and since their perfect soundness lay in obeying God and following the way He showed them, it was by forsaking the law that they were corrupted — in which Moses indirectly reproves their ingratitude, as one who had thrown away his labour upon such despisers of pious instruction.

themes: gather unto me all the elders of your tribes, and your officers
call heaven and earth to record against them
Moses spake in the ears of all the congregation the words of this song
